description: Equilibrium price, how shortages and surpluses self-correct, and the three functions of the price mechanism.
content_html:
Where Price Comes From

Every price you see — the cost of a litre of petrol, a pint of milk, a streaming subscription — is the result of demand and supply pushing against each other until they settle. That settling point is called the equilibrium price. At this price, the market “clears”: every seller who wants to sell at that price finds a buyer, and every buyer who wants to buy at that price finds a seller. The matching quantity is called the equilibrium quantity.

Think of a street market selling fresh strawberries. The stall holder sets out 200 punnets each morning. If customers are willing to buy exactly 200 punnets at, say, £2 each, the market clears perfectly. The price is at equilibrium. But markets rarely sit perfectly still — prices and quantities are always being nudged by new information, changing tastes and shifting costs.

Key Fact

At equilibrium, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. If price is above equilibrium there is a surplus (excess supply); if price is below equilibrium there is a shortage (excess demand). In both cases, market forces push price back towards equilibrium.

Excess Demand: When Price is Too Low

Imagine a new games console launches at £300. At that price, one million consumers want to buy one — but manufacturers have only produced 600,000 units. Quantity demanded (1,000,000) exceeds quantity supplied (600,000). This gap is called excess demand, or a shortage. Shoppers start bidding up the price, and some will pay £400 or more on resale sites. Meanwhile, the high price signals to producers that it is profitable to make more consoles. As price rises, demand contracts and supply extends until the two meet again at the new equilibrium.

The key chain runs like this: price too low → shortage → price rises → demand contracts, supply extends → equilibrium restored. Notice that this happens automatically without any government instruction — buyers competing to obtain the good and sellers eager to profit both push towards the clearing price.

Excess Supply: When Price is Too High

Now picture a supermarket that priced its own-brand orange juice at £2.50 a carton last winter. At that price, shoppers bought 10,000 cartons a week, but the supermarket stocked 14,000. The unsold 4,000 cartons are called excess supply, or a surplus. Stock piles up in the warehouse. To shift it, the supermarket cuts the price to £1.80. Lower prices attract more buyers (demand extends) and the supermarket orders less from its supplier (supply contracts) until equilibrium is reached again.

The chain here runs: price too high → surplus → price falls → demand extends, supply contracts → equilibrium restored. Both adjustment processes happen through the ordinary decisions of self-interested buyers and sellers, not through a central planner telling anyone what to do.

When price changes, buyers and sellers respond by moving along their existing demand and supply curves. This is called a contraction or extension of demand (or supply) — the curve itself stays where it is, and only the point on it changes.

A shift is different. It happens when something other than price changes — for example, consumer incomes rise, a new technology cuts production costs, or a health scare reduces demand. The whole curve moves left or right, creating a new equilibrium at a different price and quantity. A common exam error is writing “demand increased because price fell” — that is a movement, not a shift. Price changes cause movements; non-price factors cause shifts.

The Price Mechanism: Three Functions

Price does not just record where the market has settled — it actively guides resources to where they are most valued. Economists describe this as the price mechanism. It performs three linked functions.

Rationing. When a good is scarce, a rising price rations it among the consumers who value it most highly (and can afford to pay). During the petrol shortages of autumn 2021, rising forecourt prices — and the prospect of even higher prices — rationed available fuel, discouraging casual journeys and reserving supply for essential users. Not everyone agrees this is fair, but it is how a free market limits consumption when supply is short.

Signalling. Price changes send signals to producers and consumers about where resources are needed. When the price of electric-vehicle batteries fell sharply as production scaled up, it signalled to carmakers that the technology had become commercially viable. Investment in EV production surged. Conversely, when the price of a crop like wheat rises sharply after a poor harvest, it signals farmers around the world to plant more next season.

Incentives. Higher profits attract new firms into a market; losses push them out. If house prices in a city are high and rising, construction firms have an incentive to build more homes. Resources — land, bricklayers, materials — flow towards housebuilding because the profit signal is strong. Over time, the increased supply of homes moderates the price rise. The incentive function keeps the economy self-correcting.

Key Fact

The price mechanism allocates resources through three functions: rationing (limiting consumption when supply is scarce), signalling (communicating where resources are needed), and incentives (attracting profit-seeking producers into expanding markets). Together, these functions allow the market to coordinate millions of individual decisions without central planning.

How a New Equilibrium Forms After a Shift

Markets rarely stay in equilibrium for long. When demand or supply shifts, the old equilibrium price becomes either too high or too low, and the market adjusts to a new one. Let’s trace two real-world examples in words.

Demand shifts right (rises). Suppose a health study is published showing that oat milk reduces cholesterol. Demand for oat milk rises sharply at every price — the demand curve shifts to the right. At the old price, there is now excess demand: supermarket shelves empty and producers face waiting lists. The price is bid upwards. Rising prices contract demand back slightly and extend supply (producers work longer shifts, source more oats). Eventually a new equilibrium forms: higher price, higher quantity than before.

Supply shifts left (falls). Now suppose a drought reduces the wheat harvest. The supply of bread falls — the supply curve shifts left. At the old price, there is excess demand: more loaves wanted than are available. Price rises. Higher prices ration bread, and consumers buy slightly less (demand contracts). A new equilibrium forms: higher price, lower quantity. This is why a bad harvest year consistently pushes up food prices in supermarkets.

Total revenue is price multiplied by quantity sold. In a supply-and-demand diagram, it is represented by the rectangle formed by the equilibrium price on the vertical axis and the equilibrium quantity on the horizontal axis — that is, the area of the box from the origin to the equilibrium point.

For example, if the equilibrium price of a concert ticket is £40 and 5,000 tickets are sold, total revenue is £40 × 5,000 = £200,000. If a price rise to £50 causes quantity demanded to fall to 4,500, revenue becomes £225,000 — the firm earns more despite selling fewer tickets. Whether revenue rises or falls when price changes depends on the price elasticity of demand (covered in the next lesson).
exam_tip_html: The command words Explain and Analyse both require chains of reasoning, not isolated points. For equilibrium questions, always trace the full sequence: identify which curve shifts → state whether it shifts left or right → explain whether price and quantity rise or fall → note what happens to any surplus or shortage along the way. A very common error is confusing a movement along a curve (caused by a price change) with a shift of the curve (caused by a non-price factor). State this distinction explicitly in your answer — examiners reward it. For 9-mark evaluate questions, remember to weigh both sides: for instance, the price mechanism allocates resources efficiently in many markets but may fail where externalities exist or where consumers lack information.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Above equilibrium, excess supply pushes price down; below equilibrium, excess demand pushes price up — both forces automatically restore the market to a new clearing price.
  • The price mechanism performs three functions — rationing (limiting consumption when supply is scarce), signalling (telling producers where resources are needed) and creating incentives (attracting firms into profitable markets) — without any central direction.
  • When demand or supply shifts, the market moves to a new equilibrium. A rightward demand shift raises both price and quantity; a leftward supply shift raises price but reduces quantity. These effects ripple through related markets too.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the equilibrium price in a market?
A) The price set by the government to prevent inflation
B) The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
C) The lowest price at which a producer is willing to sell
D) The price at which all consumers are satisfied with what they pay
practice_questions.marks: B) The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A market for takeaway coffee is in equilibrium at £3.50 per cup, with 8,000 cups sold each day. Calculate the total daily revenue for sellers in this market.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct method (Total Revenue = Price × Quantity, i.e. £3.50 × 8,000); 1 mark for the correct answer of £28,000.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a shortage in a market leads to a rise in price.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a shortage means quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price; 1 mark for explaining that buyers compete for the limited supply and are willing to pay more (price is bid upwards); 1 mark for explaining that the rising price contracts demand and extends supply until equilibrium is restored.

practice_questions.text: A popular video game is launched at £50. Demand is 2 million units but only 1.2 million have been produced. Explain how the price mechanism will work to remove this shortage and restore equilibrium in the market.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying excess demand / shortage (0.8 million units); 1 mark for explaining that buyers bid the price upwards above £50; 1 mark for explaining that the higher price signals to producers that it is profitable to increase supply (supply extends along the curve); 1 mark for explaining that higher price also causes some consumers to leave the market (demand contracts) until quantity demanded once again equals quantity supplied at the new equilibrium price.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a sharp increase in the cost of coffee beans affects the equilibrium price and quantity in the UK coffee shop market.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A developed, sequenced chain of reasoning. Rising bean costs increase producers' costs of production, shifting the supply curve to the left at every price. At the old equilibrium price there is now excess demand — coffee shops cannot profitably supply the same quantity. This bidding process pushes the equilibrium price upward. Higher prices cause consumers to contract their demand (some switch to tea or home-brewed alternatives), while the limited supply available at the higher price brings quantity supplied and demanded back into balance at a new equilibrium: higher price, lower quantity than before. The student may also note revenue implications or the signal to consumers to cut consumption.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correct identification of a leftward supply shift with a clear chain noting higher price and lower quantity. Some explanation of the adjustment mechanism but less fully developed.

Developing (1–2 marks): Identifies supply falls or price rises but without a clear connected chain.

practice_questions.text:
"The price mechanism is the most effective way to allocate resources in an economy."
Evaluate this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): A well-balanced argument with a clear supported judgement. Arguments in favour: the price mechanism allocates resources automatically and efficiently without central planning; price signals guide resources to where they are most valued (e.g. profit in high-demand markets attracts new firms); rationing prevents excess consumption when supply is scarce; prices respond quickly to new information. Arguments against: the price mechanism can fail when externalities exist (e.g. pollution — private cost is lower than social cost, so too much is produced); it may ration by ability to pay rather than need (e.g. housing, healthcare), raising fairness concerns; imperfect information can distort price signals; it may not provide public goods (non-rival, non-excludable) because no price can be charged. Judgement: the answer should conclude which side is stronger and why, using an 'it depends on' framework — for example, 'In markets for private goods with good information, the price mechanism works well; it is less effective where externalities or information failures are significant.'

Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides present with some development; judgement reached but may not be fully supported.

Developing (3–4 marks): One-sided or limited development; judgement absent or unsupported.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple relevant points only; no analytical chain.

options: The price at which producers maximise their profit
The price set by the government in a regulated market
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
The lowest price any consumer is willing to pay

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an example of the signalling function of the price mechanism?
options: A higher price for petrol reduces the number of journeys made by drivers
Falling battery prices communicate to carmakers that electric vehicle technology is commercially viable
A government sets a maximum price to keep rents affordable
A fall in price causes consumers to buy more of a good

knowledge_checks.q: When the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied at the current price, there is _____ in the market.
The price mechanism allocates resources through rationing, signalling, and creating _____ for producers to expand supply.
Match each market situation to its outcome:
right: Excess supply — price falls back to equilibrium
Excess demand — price rises back to equilibrium
New equilibrium at higher price and higher quantity

flashcard_questions.q: What is the equilibrium price in a market?
flashcard_questions.a: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, clearing the market.

flashcard_questions.q: What is excess demand, and what does it do to price?
flashcard_questions.a: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price; it pushes price upwards.

flashcard_questions.q: What is excess supply, and what does it do to price?
flashcard_questions.a: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the current price; it pushes price downwards.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three functions of the price mechanism.
flashcard_questions.a: Rationing (limiting consumption when supply is scarce), signalling (communicating where resources are needed), and creating incentives (attracting producers into profitable markets).

flashcard_questions.q: What does the rationing function of price mean?
flashcard_questions.a: Rising prices limit consumption when supply is scarce, reserving goods for those who value them most.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the signalling function of price do for producers?
flashcard_questions.a: It tells producers where resources are needed — a high price signals profitable opportunities to expand.

flashcard_questions.q: A demand curve shifts right. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
flashcard_questions.a: Both equilibrium price and quantity rise.

flashcard_questions.q: A supply curve shifts left. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
flashcard_questions.a: Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a movement along a demand curve and a shift of it?
flashcard_questions.a: A movement is caused by a price change; a shift is caused by a non-price factor such as income or tastes.

flashcard_questions.q: Calculate total revenue when price is £40 per unit and 5,000 units are sold.
Why does a surplus cause the price to fall?
flashcard_questions.a: Sellers have unsold stock and reduce price to attract buyers, contracting supply and extending demand.

flashcard_questions.q: The equilibrium quantity is _____ — the amount bought and sold when the market clears.
flashcard_questions.a: The quantity where demand equals supply.

glossary_terms.definition: The price at which the quantity that consumers want to buy exactly equals the quantity that producers want to sell, leaving no surplus and no shortage.
The amount of a good bought and sold in a market when it is in equilibrium — the quantity where demand equals supply.
A situation in which the quantity demanded of a good exceeds the quantity supplied at the current price, creating upward pressure on price.
A situation in which the quantity supplied of a good exceeds the quantity demanded at the current price, creating downward pressure on price.
The way in which price changes transmit information, ration scarce goods and create incentives, allocating resources across the economy without central direction.
